power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Challenges associated with supporting a child with a neurodevelopmental condition (NDC) may mean that wellbeing among these families is subject to different dynamics than among other families.
In this study, we modelled a shared basis for family wellbeing in the Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Cohort Study (MoBa) using measures of life satisfaction, depression, and anxiety.

Next, we tested for structural differences in the shared basis of family wellbeing between different groups of families of children diagnosed with an NDC and comparison families without diagnoses using multi-group structural equation modelling.

Finally, we examined how measures of children's, mothers', and fathers' genetic liabilities to neurodevelopmental conditions and related traits were associated with wellbeing and whether these associations differed by group.
We identified two well-fitting models that parameterised a shared basis for family wellbeing.
Structurally, family wellbeing was similar between almost all NDC-diagnosis groups and the comparison group.
The exception was the autism-diagnosis group, where the pattern of links between different family members' wellbeing factors differed significantly to that of the comparison group.
Any other group differences were related to the overall level of wellbeing or lower-level patterns of reporting on life satisfaction, depression, and anxiety.
Mothers', fathers', and children's indices of genetic liability to various traits were associated with wellbeing, typically via their own wellbeing or a shared family wellbeing factor.
However, we did not observe any differences in genetic associations between NDC-diagnosis and comparison families.

A similar, shared familial basis for wellbeing between families with and without children with NDC diagnoses indicates that the specific dynamics of wellbeing in families remain consistent, even as levels of overall wellbeing may differ.
This finding may have implications for the kind of support that can be offered to improve wellbeing among families of individuals diagnosed with NDCs.

Families of children with a neurodevelopmental condition (NDC) often face unique challenges involving understanding and supporting their neurodivergent child's particular strengths and difficulties, navigating and advocating for their child in complex systems of health, care, and educational support, and managing time for work and social activities (Tint & Weiss, 2016; Whitehead et al., 2015).

text.text: Given the high heritability of NDCs (Faraone & Larsson, 2019; Lichtenstein et al., 2010; Tick et al., 2016), some researchers have used genetic information to try to understand family wellbeing in the context of NDCs.

text.text: However, there is a clear lack of research using genetic liabilities to NDCs and related traits in both parents and children to examine the dynamics of family wellbeing as a whole.
In this study, we aim to investigate the shared basis of family wellbeing in the context of diagnosed NDCs and related genetic liabilities.

To this end, we use questionnaire, genomic, and health-registry data of Norwegian families to A) model the shared basis of family wellbeing; B) understand how genetic variants associated with NDCs and related traits are linked to family wellbeing; C) test for structural differences in the shared basis of wellbeing between families of children with an NDC diagnosis and comparison families without these diagnoses; and D) assess whether the genetic contributions are different between these groups.

text.text: Participants were recruited from all over Norway from 1999-2008.
The women consented to participation in 41% of the pregnancies.
The cohort includes approximately 114.500 children, 95.200 mothers and 75.200 fathers.
MoBa is regulated by the Norwegian Health Registry Act.

text.text: We grouped the full sample into families by linking together all children of the same mother.
After assignment of an index child in each family (see below under 2.2.2 NDC diagnoses), we randomly selected one sibling per family (where available) to be retained for analysis in a sibling sample.
Where available, we included data of the index child's father.
To measure family wellbeing, we used scales for life satisfaction, depression, and anxiety for each family member.
All children's and mothers' items were reported by mothers in the year the child turned 8, whereas fathers' items were reported by fathers themselves in 2015 (regardless of their child's age).
See supplementary materials for details on outcome measure scales and internal consistency.

For all outcomes, scale scores were calculated by calculating a mean score of all non-missing items and multiplying this score by the number of items in the scale, if at least half the items were non-missing.
All items showed good to excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .75-.94; see Supplementary Table S2).
text.formatted: All items showed good to excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .75-.94; see Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: We identified all children who have received a diagnosis of an NDC at least at two occasions according to NPR and assigned them (or, if multiple children qualified, randomly assigned one) to be the index child.
We did this for any NDC, ADHD, and autism.
For ADHD and autism, we also created subgroups by removing families of index children with both ADHD and autism diagnosis (i.e., creating ADHD-only and autism-only groups).
We also split the any-NDCdiagnosis group into families of earlier (i.e., ≤ 10 years) and later (i.e., > 10 years) diagnosed index children.
text.formatted: We also split the any-NDCdiagnosis group into families of earlier (i.e., ≤ 10 years) and later (i.e., > 10 years) diagnosed index children.

text.text: Finally, we grouped all families together who did not have a child diagnosed with an NDC during follow-up in NPR (henceforth the comparison group) and assigned one child at random from each of these families to act as the "index" child.
For each family member, we calculated polygenic indices (PGIs) for a range of neurodevelopmental conditions and related traits.

PGI reflect a person's genetic liability for a trait, based on a weighted sum of the effects of common genetic variants on that trait or condition in prior a genome-wide association study (GWAS; Pingault et al., 2022).

text.text: We calculated PGI based on summary statistics from the most recent well-powered GWAS based on samples European-like ancestry for ADHD (Demontis et al., 2023), autism (Grove et al., 2019), anxiety (Strom et al., 2026), cognitive ability (Savage et al., 2018), depression (Adams et al., 2025), neuroticism (Nagel et al., 2018), schizophrenia (Trubetskoy et al., 2022), and wellbeing (Baselmans et al., 2019) using weights estimated by LDpred-auto model in the LDpred2 software (Privé et al., 2021).

text.text: To parameterise a shared basis of family wellbeing, we used structural equation modelling (SEM) to test whether underlying (latent) family variables could explain the variance-covariance structure of life satisfaction, depression, and anxiety in children, mothers, fathers, and siblings.
We specified 5 hypothesised factor models with varying numbers of latent variables and factor structures.

These were 1) Single factor; in which all observed variables from all family members loaded on a single common factor; 2) Correlated factors; in which observed variables for each family member loaded on correlated individual factors; 3) Two-level; in which correlations in (2) were replaced with an overarching factor; 4) Domain-specific correlated factors; and 5) Domainspecific two-level; which were structured as per (2) and ( 3), but with factors linked to traits rather than family members.
text.formatted: These were 1) Single factor; in which all observed variables from all family members loaded on a single common factor; 2) Correlated factors; in which observed variables for each family member loaded on correlated individual factors; 3) Two-level; in which correlations in (2) were replaced with an overarching factor; 4) Domain-specific correlated factors; and 5) Domainspecific two-level; which were structured as per (2) and ( <ref type="formula">3</ref>), but with factors linked to traits rather than family members.

text.text: For a graphical overview of these models, see supplementary figures S1-5.
All models included the child's sex and birth year, and the sibling's birth year as covariates.

We assessed the fit of each model using a chi-square test and a selection of fit indices, including the comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis index (TLI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), standardised root mean square residual (SRMR), Akaike information criteria (AIC), and Bayesian information criterion (BIC).
We considered CFI and TLI values over .95 and RMSEA and SRMR values below .06 to be indicative of good fit.
AIC and BIC were used to compare all 5 models, where models with the lowest AIC and BIC values were preferred.
All models with acceptable fit were carried forward in our downstream analyses.
Next, we tested whether family members' genetic liability to a range of neurodevelopmental conditions and related traits predicted latent family wellbeing.

To do this, we extended each of our selected models from the previous step, by regressing the highest-order latent wellbeing factor(s) onto fathers', mothers', and children's polygenic indices for ADHD, anxiety, autism, cognitive functioning, depression, neuroticism, schizophrenia, and wellbeing, simultaneously.

For each family member we compared this model to a model in which we constrained all genetic effects of that family member to be 0 and assessed the resultant loss of fit using likelihood ratio tests (LRT).

Because LRTs are highly sensitive to small changes in fit when sample sizes are large, we also assessed differences in CFI and RMSEA, where changes exceeding ΔCFI = -.01 or ΔRMSEA = .015 were considered indicative of a substantial loss of fit based on standard benchmarks (Chen, 2007).

text.text: Significant (LRT) and substantial (ΔCFI/ ΔRMSEA) loss of fit from constraining the genetic effects would indicate that genetic liabilities associated with neurodevelopmental conditions and related traits affect family wellbeing via direct and/or indirect effects.

To assess whether the structure of family wellbeing was similar for families of children with or without different NDC diagnoses, we ran the models of family wellbeing taken forward from 2.3.1 using a measurement invariance framework (Putnick & Bornstein, 2016) .

text.text: For each group comparison, we first ran a model in which all parameters were freely estimated.

We then progressively constrained the model by forcing first only factor loadings, then additionally latent covariances, observed variable intercepts, and finally all parameters including latent means to be the same between groups.
After each additional constraint, we assessed the change in fit using LRT, ΔCFI, and ΔRMSEA according to the thresholds reported in 2.3.2.
For each of the NDCdiagnosis groups (see 2.2.2), we performed multigroup comparison against the comparison group.
Additionally, we compared the earlier-diagnosed group to the later-diagnosed group.
Comparisons between groups with severely unbalanced sample sizes (i.e., exceeding a 2:1 ratio) risk not being able to detect group differences (Yoon & Lai, 2018).
text.formatted: Comparisons between groups with severely unbalanced sample sizes (i.e., exceeding a 2:1 ratio) risk not being able to detect group differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Yoon & Lai, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: As such, we ran 100 iterations of each model on a random subsample from the larger group matching the sample size (and number of siblings) from the smaller group.
We then took the average of the change in fit indices across all models for inference.
This was the case for all group comparisons, except for the more balanced earlier-vs. later-diagnosed comparison.

Finally, we compared models including genetic factors between all groups specified in section 2.3.3. to assess whether genetic effects on the shared basis of family wellbeing are different between different groups of families.
For each group comparison, we ran one instance of each model where all parameters were freely estimated, and one where the genetic effects were constrained to be equal between groups.
We conducted an LRT and calculated change in fit as described above to assess whether genetic effects on the shared basis of family wellbeing were different between groups.

text.text: Here we examined the shared basis of family wellbeing and the extent to which its structure differs between different NDC-diagnosis subgroups and a comparison group in the MoBa cohort.

We identified two theoretical models of shared family wellbeing that explained the correlations between observational measures of wellbeing in children, mothers, fathers, and siblings in our data adequately.
We found associations of family members' genetic liabilities to neurodevelopmental conditions and related traits on both their own and, in the case of mothers, other family members' wellbeing.
Finally, we found that family wellbeing is broadly structurally and genetically similar between families of children with diagnosed NDCs and those with children without diagnoses of these conditions.

The primary exception was that the covariance structure of family wellbeing was different between families of autistic children and families of typically developing children, although this seemed to be driven by relatively small differences between the two groups across all correlations rather than one or a few significant differences.
Otherwise, group differences were found only in terms of the levels of observed anxiety, depression, and life satisfaction, rather than the way family members' wellbeing was interrelated.
From our five pre-specified models, only the two models with wellbeing factors for each family member fitted the data well.

In contrast, the models in which the observed variables loaded either directly onto a latent factor for overall family wellbeing, or onto domain-specific (i.e., family anxiety, family depression, and family life satisfaction) latent factors, did not fit the data well.
This suggests that family wellbeing associates between family members at a higher level, rather than at a domain-specific level.

In other words, higher anxiety for one family member's anxiety might not be specifically associated higher anxiety of other family members, but instead might be related to their broader wellbeing via the individual's own general wellbeing.
This is in line with findings from a previous study suggesting that the associations between family members' mental health symptoms are not domain-specific (Jiang et al., 2025).

text.text: Our genetic models showed several different genetic contributions to family wellbeing.
In our correlated factors model, we found associations between several parental and child PGIs and their own wellbeing factors.

Children's wellbeing was negatively associated with their own PGI for cognitive functioning and negatively with their own PGI for neuroticism, whereas parents' wellbeing was negatively associated with their own PGIs for depression and neuroticism, and positively with their PGI for wellbeing.

We found cross-family member associations for mothers only, with maternal PGIs for autism and depression being negatively associated with father's wellbeing, the maternal PGI for cognitive functioning being negatively associated with index children's wellbeing, and the maternal PGI for wellbeing being positively associated with index children's and siblings' wellbeing.
We also observed similar associations between these maternal PGIs and the higher-level family wellbeing factor in the Two-level model.

It is notable that different measures of genetic liability were associated with parents and children's own wellbeing, which could reflect changes in genetic contributions to wellbeing across the lifespan.

This is in line with findings from previous research where the associations between specific PGIs and emotional and behavioural problems change over time (Bakken et al., 2025; Shakeshaft et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This is in line with findings from previous research where the associations between specific PGIs and emotional and behavioural problems change over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bakken et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Shakeshaft et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, in our study, these differences can also be explained by parents self-reporting on their wellbeing whereas children's wellbeing was reported by mothers using a different set of scales.

The finding that maternal PGIs were predominant in explaining variation in shared familial wellbeing is also somewhat consistent with previous results from Jiang et al. (2025), who found a central role of maternal depressive feelings within a network analysis of family mental health.

(2025)</ref>, who found a central role of maternal depressive feelings within a network analysis of family mental health.

text.text: An important caveat, again, is that mothers reported on their own, the index child's, and sibling's wellbeing, meaning that maternal PGI effects on family wellbeing might also capture variance that is due to reporting tendencies, it is notable that maternal PGI effects on fathers' (self-reported) wellbeing were also found in the model where these were tested for.
We found that the structure of family wellbeing, as modelled using our data, varied relatively little in the context of neurodevelopmental conditions.
The exception to this general rule was that wellbeing factors of individual members of families from the autism-diagnosis group were differentially correlated than those of comparison families.

The common pattern of differences that appeared to drive this result was a reduction in the magnitude of the associations between mothers', fathers', and index children's wellbeing and that of the nonindex siblings (.30/-.05/.22), relative to the same parameters from the model of comparison families (.37/.14/.60), although the index child-father correlation was also changed markedly (.31 vs .12).

To interpret this finding, it is first important to emphasise that none of these parameters were directly statistically compared; hence, their collective effect on the relative fit of the constrained vs. unconstrained models is the only robust basis for inference.

Moreover, the apparent importance of the sibling correlations indicate the effect should be interpreted with caution, since this was among the smallest groups in the models (N=725 for the autism group).
With these caveats aside, taken at face value this finding indicates a somewhat different basis for wellbeing among families of autistic children that could warrant further investigation.

While structurally similar in terms of wellbeing, we found that families from the other NDC-diagnosed groups differed to families in the comparison group by reporting, on average, lower wellbeing than families from the comparison group.

This is in line with previous research showing that caregivers of children diagnosed with an NDC report lower quality of life and increased mental health difficulties (Garrido et al., 2025; Masefield et al., 2020; Scherer et al., 2019; Schnabel et al., 2020).

text.text: For the NDC-diagnosis subgroups, we observed that the baseline scores for observed life satisfaction, depression, and anxiety were different between each subgroup and comparison families.
That is, for similar levels of latent wellbeing, questionnaire item responses were different for subgroups of families of NDC-diagnosed children than comparison families.

We also observed that wellbeing for families of later-diagnosed (i.e., later than 10 years) children is higher than that for families of earlier-diagnosed children, which may partially be explained by early-diagnosed children experiencing more difficulties in early childhood (Hrdlicka et al., 2024), although this relationship is likely confounded in complex ways (Glaser et al., 2026) -including the relationship between earlier diagnosis and earlier provision of support.

text.text: However, these results could also be due to the timing of the questionnaires, as index children's and mother's questionnaires were taken when the index child was 8 years old.

Within the same cohort, but focusing only on children with an autism diagnosis, the observational relationship between age at autism diagnosis and wellbeing show a similar pattern at age 8, but an inverse pattern when outcomes are measured at 14 years (Glaser et al., 2026).

text.text: Finally, we found no differences in genetic associations with wellbeing for any of the group comparisons.
While an absence of evidence for differences is not equivalent to demonstrating genetic similarity, a lack of genetic differences is consistent with the broad structural similarity described above.
This study is subject to some limitations.

First, the cohort includes an overrepresentation of families with higher socioeconomic backgrounds and education levels, and these participants have higher response rates over time (Vejrup et al., 2022).
text.formatted: First, the cohort includes an overrepresentation of families with higher socioeconomic backgrounds and education levels, and these participants have higher response rates over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Vejrup et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: As such, it is important to consider potential selection and attrition biases (Biele et al., 2019).
text.formatted: As such, it is important to consider potential selection and attrition biases <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Biele et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Second, mothers reported on their own, but also the index children's and siblings' outcomes, which could introduce common method bias and inflate correlations between variables because they were reported on by the same person (Podsakoff et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Second, mothers reported on their own, but also the index children's and siblings' outcomes, which could introduce common method bias and inflate correlations between variables because they were reported on by the same person <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Podsakoff et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Third, for each group of family members, all outcomes came from a single point in time, although the difference between those time points may have differed substantially between families.

That is, index children's and mothers' outcomes were measured when the index child was 8 years old, fathers' outcomes were measured in 2015 regardless of their child's age, and siblings' outcomes were measured when the sibling was 8 years old.

Although we tried to adjust for these differences by including index children's and siblings' birth year as covariates, this adjustment is unlikely to have perfectly accounted for these measurement discrepancies.

Fourth, complete ascertainment of sibling data was not possible, meaning siblings were not completely representative of the true sibling population, limiting our ability to confidently interpret sibling effects.
Finally, because this was a crosssectional design, it is possible that associations may not persist over time.
As such, future research should aim to employ longitudinal designs, potentially looking at factors associated with stability and change in family wellbeing over time.

In this study, we found that family wellbeing in the MoBa cohort is best described by models with interrelated latent wellbeing factors for each individual family member, suggesting a familial basis for wellbeing.

We found that family wellbeing modelled in this way was broadly genetically and structurally similar regardless of whether or not families included a child with a diagnosed neurodevelopmental condition.

Where differences in these families were observed, they primarily involved lower overall wellbeing or differential reporting on constituent measures of wellbeing (life satisfaction, depression, and anxiety).

The finding that family members' wellbeing is intrinsically interlinked -and in a broadly consistent way irrespective of diagnosed neurodevelopmental conditions among children -suggests that support is likely to be more effective when the family is considered as a whole, rather than focussed on a single family member, so that index children, parents, and siblings are all considered.

Families of children with an NDC reported lower wellbeing on average, which may reflect differences in the specific stressors faced by these families, rather than differences in how family wellbeing is structured.

Longitudinal studies are needed to establish the direction of influence between family members and to identify intra-familial (e.g., caregiving demands) and extra-familial stressors (e.g., navigating complex systems of care, stigma, advocating for a child's needs) that might impact family wellbeing.

What is known • Family members of children with a neurodevelopmental condition often report lower wellbeing compared to families of typically developing children, though there has been little investigation into differences in the specific dynamics of family wellbeing.
What is new?
• The structure of family wellbeing is broadly similar between families of children with and without a neurodevelopmental condition.
• Families of children with a neurodevelopmental condition typically experienced lower overall wellbeing or reported more depression and anxiety symptoms or lower life satisfaction.
What is relevant?

• The interrelatedness of individual family members' wellbeing -irrespective of neurodevelopmental condition diagnoses among children -supports familylevel approaches targeting wellbeing and motivates longitudinal research on the direction of influence between family members.
